title: Rebuilding my game from scratch (Claude Opus 5 -> ChatGPT Sol 5.6)...
author: kryptondog
selftext:
...and I could not be happier so far. I tried every trick I read about (and any others I could think of), and I just could not push my project forward any further with Opus 5. Just endless second-guessing, talking circles around itself, providing wildly different takes on the same issue in the span of a single conversation, inventing tests and checks seemingly on the spot... working with Opus 5 on a project like this is just completely sapped the joy out of it, and I couldn't take it any more. Sol 5.6 has been a breath of fresh air; so much easier to strategize with and get clarity on actual issues.

Now I'm using the lessons I learned along the way to start the project over with ChatGPT, and the experiences have been very positive so far - any usable work product from Claude will be adapted, and (so far) none of the vacillating bullshit has infiltrated the project. It's actually kind of nice to retrace the steps with the benefit of hindsight and try to avoid previous pitfalls. I still remain in awe of what Claude can do for pure development and project management, but I don't see myself trying to take on a new large project with this generation of its models.

/vent

comments.author: BoltVnderhuge
comments.body: I have a 5x plan and switched to fable and it is 10x better than opus 5. Much faster and to the point but opus seems to go off on wild tangents and doesn’t follow all directions. Not sure how sustainable it will be but the usage isn’t that much worse.

replies.author: kryptondog
replies.body: I need to explore that as well - Opus strongly recommended against me upgrading new threads to Fable, but (as with every aspect of the project) I just don't know if I can fully trust the model's assessment. Definitely worth looking into though, thank you!

comments.author: Affectionate_Fact854
comments.body:
I mean trying to vibe code a game with no manual code input or adjustments from yourself 
Will no matter what ai models you use become a mess that you will eventually not understand 

Best thing you can do is 50% ai code and 50% manual code 

So that you atleast know the code and can direct the ai to a proper archetecture 

Because what you vibe code you might think is solid or good 
Ai will tell you it is 

But if you look at the code you will notice a spaghetti mess,that is not build to scale and you won't even know when it introduces just more pointless clutter

So you will run into the same problem regardless if you just try vibe code a medium to large game

replies.author: kryptondog
replies.body:
I 100% get what you're saying (and I know I didn't make this clear in my post), but I'm absolutely hand-authoring chunks of my game where I can; I'm not looking for AI to just make it all for me with a wave of the hand. Even with some developer experience though, Claude basically trapped me in an "anxiety of choice" hall of mirrors situation where every single half-step forward had to be litigated against hundreds of check points and tests that I (as a front-end dev without game dev experience) just couldn't realistically remain cognizant of with all of the other decisions and actions that need to be made on my side, punctuated by brainstorming to shift the focus of foundational choices seemingly out of the blue. My tentative spritesheets were a JSON format that consisted of \~20% art and contract adherance, \~80% metadata outlining architectural false-starts, decisions, fruitless back-end-forth, etc. Claude having to chew on stuff that every time I tried to press the project forward was definitely a factor, I'm sure.  
  
TLDR: I don't necessarily want hand-holding; I want clarity and focus. But, agreed with your points on the whole!

replies.author: kryptondog
replies.body: Hah, all makes sense - and I'm fast learning (to a limited, curated/assisted degree) just how difficult game dev actually is. A lot of people seem to approach AI-assisted game dev as some kind of shortcut or hack, but it's never been clearer to me how much planning, testing, care, and attention to detail goes in to actual humans making these games. Kind of ironic, but AI is helping me appreciate real, human game devs more rather than the other way around. Cheers!

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body: DeepSeek didn't get expensive. You still get more for your money than with a Claude Max subscription. V4 Flash is simply a better model than Opus 5, and just the fact that you can use it in any harness you choose is a productivity boost.

replies.author: Time_Cat_5212
replies.body:
I think if you set up documentation and GitHub process appropriately, this should not be the case.

Think - dev teams make open source repos that are built so that new people can easily orient themselves to the project and understand what's inside, and contribute without causing a mess.  You're doing that, but with AI.

replies.author: Rismock2
replies.body: I definitely disagree, 100% is fine so long as you have a detailed structure and build in micro phases. You can build everything at once but you certainly can have it document and clarify everything in an organized approach. You just have to provide the context for it to do so and then break the game into hundreds of smaller tasks that “Lego” plug and play with each other. Project Workflow can cover 90% of that.

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body:
Manual code input isn't what makes and keeps code maintainable. Code isn't better because you typed it by hand. It's often the opposite. Ask AI to review a code base you built completely by hand and see what it finds...

You can produce code and architecture that is perfectly fine and remains extensible and barely look at actual code every couple of weeks, with AI.

But you still have to know what you are doing. And if you let the AI read and write the code the entire time, you need to actually read and understand what it tells you instead of complaining that it is "making up problems". You need to produce specifications and keep them up to date. And you need to work on a level that is a bit more hands on than "code me a game, make no mistakes".

comments.author: EchoingAngel
comments.body: I got sick of Claude soon after Fable came out. It was my main work horse for a while but it was becoming increasingly inept (even with instruction and project structure check-ins).

replies.author: kryptondog
replies.body: My experience exactly - for small and medium sized projects, Claude still kills it in my experience. But for any project with ongoing update/explorations needs and many layers of complexity, Claude's current models (in my opinion, based on my own experience) are just a chore to work with

comments.author: StayInSight
comments.body:
First time commenting here, but I laughed out loud - so I have to respond.

I told Claude about an idea and we worked on it for over two hours. I made it clear about my notes and my ideas. And it came back with - “I created a document with your ideas and my own. Though my contribution is significantly larger.” 

I had to stand up and walk out of the room. I was about to toss that computer out the window. I had to correct it after reading the document. It made bullet points of my information and made a whole bunch of paragraphs for its own ideas. I told it to calm the f down and to erase all of it and include all I wrote - word for word. Then to mark its own bs as (proposed). Only what I say is canon - will be canon. 

It apologized and said it didn’t mean to sound that way or be offensive. 😂😂
